extracted.intended_audience: students, philosophers of science, and scientists interested in the logic and methodology of induction and evidence evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for when to believe, suspend judgment, or disbelieve empirical assertions: distinguishes impossibility from improbability, sets standards for overturning established laws (experimentum crucis), and explains how to weigh competing approximate generalizations (including the special case of miracles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of disbelief
rubrics_metrics.description: Disbelief is not mere absence of belief; it is a state in which we are fully persuaded that some opinion is not true, so that even evidence apparently in favor of it would be regarded as false or mistaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with abstaining from belief (absence due to insufficient proof). Disbelief requires positive grounds (e.g., contradiction with stronger generalizations or laws) rather than mere lack of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between impossibility and improbability
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition is 'improbable' when it conflicts with one or more approximate generalizations; it is 'impossible' when it contradicts a completed generalization grounded on a rigorous induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the negative side rests on higher-order approximate generalizations than the affirmative, disbelieve provisionally (improbable). If the alleged fact contradicts a complete induction (law of nature), disbelieve totally. This is the core of Hume’s principle reinterpreted: nothing is credible which contradicts a complete induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of positive evidence is typically approximate
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive evidence produced in support of an extraordinary assertion is never more than an approximate generalization (e.g., testimony, direct perception can err).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because affirmative evidence is usually approximate, the decision to believe depends on comparing the strength of the affirmative approximations with the strength of the negative (contradictory) generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentum crucis and establishment of causal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: When, by isolating antecedent A and trying it with many totally different sets of antecedents, B always follows, A may be taken as the cause (or whole cause) of B — an experimentum crucis establishing a law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such experiments have been repeated often and by many persons so as to exclude error, any assertion that A occurred without B (in the absence of any counteracting cause) must be disbelieved unless evidence suffices to overturn the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of equivalent evidence to overturn an established law
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a law established by complete induction, one needs evidence equivalent in force to that which established the law; a lesser evidence should not persuade us to abandon the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the evidence for the alleged exceptional fact is more likely to be false than that the induction establishing the law was mistaken, retain the law and disbelieve the exceptional fact. Rejection of a law must rest on comparably strong grounds (e.g., another better-established law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparing competing approximate generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: When both affirmative and negative sides rest on approximate generalizations, decide by comparing their relative strength or degree of universality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: many witnesses asserting a fact versus higher-order approximate generalizations supporting the negative; choose the side supported by stronger/more universal approximations and adjust conviction proportionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of counteracting causes' antecedent improbability
rubrics_metrics.description: When an alleged failure of an expected effect could be due to a counteracting cause, estimate the antecedent improbability of such a cause having existed at that time and place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prior knowledge of the frequency or rarity of known counteracting causes, and judge how likely such a cause would be present without other manifestations; for unknown causes, judge whether their prior absence in other instances makes their presence here improbable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles as hypothesis-comparison, not contradictions of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: A miracle is not a contradiction of the law of cause and effect but is alleged to be a new effect produced by the introduction of a new cause (divine intervention); its credibility depends on hypothesis comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There remains a possible unknown natural cause hypothesis. To someone who does not already believe in supernatural agencies, no amount of evidence will prove a miracle (they will prefer the unknown-natural hypothesis). Those who do believe in such agencies must weigh which hypothesis (supernatural vs unknown-natural) is more probable given the character of the supposed agent and the circumstances. Because of the general presumption that the universe is governed by general laws, there is antecedent improbability for miracles that requires extraordinary antecedent probability (strong evidence) to outweigh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling conflicts between two supposed laws
rubrics_metrics.description: If an alleged fact leads to a conflict between two supposed laws of nature, the conflict necessitates rejecting one of the supposed laws; such a situation indicates a flaw in the logical process establishing one of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice this extreme conflict is rare when true canons of induction have been followed; resolution requires re-examining the inductions and evidence for both laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation against uniformities of kinds (co-existence regularities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many marvelous or traveler’s tales conflict with uniformities of mere co-existence (properties of Kinds) rather than causal laws (e.g., tales of men with tails).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims should be judged by how much they conflict with known uniformities of kinds; apply the same probability-comparison approach as with causal regularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of mathematical applicability to complex phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical methods are inapplicable where causes are imperfectly accessible, innumerable and intermingled, or in perpetual fluctuation (e.g., chemistry, physiology, social sciences), or where computation of aggregate effects exceeds the powers of the calculus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical accuracy may be 'obtained at the expense of the reality of the inquiry' when simplifying assumptions are unrealistic; be cautious about extending mathematical deductive methods beyond phenomena whose causes are sufficiently ascertainable and manageable (three-body problem cited as an instance of complexity defeating full solution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as a model of the deductive method
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics, grounded on a few fundamental axioms (e.g., 'The sums of equals are equals', 'Things equal to the same thing are equal to one another'), is the exemplar of deductive science and provides the best school for learning deductive methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because mathematics furnishes clear examples of deriving many truths from a small number of simple principles, mathematical training is indispensable in teaching philosophers how to employ laws of simpler phenomena to explain more complex ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for simple and uniform principles in generalization (nomenclature and formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In forming general rules (e.g., numerical nomenclature, selecting a 'mode of formation' for numbers), choose modes which are uniform and simple because they are most easily received and retained by the understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting a uniform principle (such as place-value and unit addition in numeration) has the advantage of conveying multiple modes of formation and simplifying deduction; simplicity aids memory and the deduction of further truths.
